seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Late July through August, once the Downey Creek approach and ridge camps melt out and glacier bridges still hold

June.reason: Deep snow still buries the off-trail approach over Itswoot Ridge and Bachelor Creek, and the east-face cracks often run wet with melt.

July.reason: The approach snow is thinning and glacier crossings are well bridged; early July can still leave snow on ledges and the base of the face.

August.reason: The east face is at its driest and the glacier approach is still passable before late-season bridges collapse and moats open.

September.reason: Cooler, drier rock, but crevasses on the approach glaciers are open and the moat at the base widens; days are noticeably shorter.

October.reason: The first fall storms bring snow and verglas to the loose, chimney-heavy pitches, and a multi-day retreat through the brush gets serious.

evidence: Gunsight area glacier bridges melt out by late Aug (Chickamin crossing turned back; bridge gone two weeks later): https://stephabegg.com/trip-reports/washington/north-gunsight-wf/
Aug ascents of Gunsight routes, 10-ft moat at the Middle/South notch: http://chriswinter.blogspot.com/2011/08/reflections-on-gunsight-range.html
Early-July trip still had snow hiking and a snow-covered ridge camp: https://wildsnow.com/20610/washingtons-gunsight-range-backcountry-climbing/

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: January to February, after a rain-to-summit warm spell is followed by a hard freeze that sets the couloir's snow and ice

November.reason: The low-elevation couloir rarely holds enough ice yet, and early storms load the north face with unbonded snow that sluffs down the line.

December.reason: Ice can start forming in the lower ribbon and steps, but the snowpack is often shallow and the approach brush and cliffs poorly covered.

January.reason: Mid-winter freeze-thaw cycles are most likely to set the couloir into firm neve and build the crux ice; the road gate adds about 2.5 miles each way.

February.reason: A deep, settled snowpack covers the lower cliffs and a thaw followed by a cold snap can leave the steps and crux pitch in solid condition.

March.reason: The route's first ascent came in early March; lengthening days help, but sun and warm spells rot the ice and trigger wet slides off the face.

April.reason: Warming releases wet avalanches, cornice fall and icefall down the north face, and the thin ice on the crux and top runnels deteriorates.

May.reason: Spring melt sends constant rock, ice and wet snow down the face; the Mountain Loop gate typically still keeps the road closed until late spring.

evidence: FA March 2, 1996; ideal after warm rain-to-summit then cold snap; serious winter avalanche hazard: https://www.mattsea.com/featured/BigFour/
AAC FA account: http://publications.americanalpineclub.org/articles/12199706000/The-Spindrift-Couloir-Scrappin-It-Up-After-Classes-in-the-Washington-Cascades

Mountain Loop Hwy gated at Deer Creek Nov-May, ~2.5 mi road walk to Big Four: https://www.fs.usda.gov/r06/mbs/alerts/mountain-loop-highway-closed-winter-season-deer-creek-bedal-campground and https://www.wta.org/go-hiking/hikes/big-four-ice-caves-snowshoe
flags: Old season was prose; set to Dec-Mar. Few recorded ascents, so month-by-month status is inferred from the route's low elevation, north aspect and the freeze-thaw requirement rather than a body of dated ascents.
Access row says no permit / no wilderness, but also mentions Glacier Peak Wilderness rules; worth a human look.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: August, when the approach to Park Creek Pass is snow-free and the icefall crossing below the face is still bridged

June.reason: Heavy snow lingers toward Park Creek Pass and on the face's ledges, and the icefall at the base is at its most active as it warms.

July.reason: The trail approach clears, but the summit gully and ledges may still hold snow and ice, and the red rock band sheds rockfall during melt.

August.reason: The only recorded ascents came in August: the face is at its driest and the small glacier and icefall are still passable on snow.

September.reason: Cooler temperatures quiet the rockfall, but the glacier goes to bare ice, the icefall crossing gets more broken and days are shorter.

October.reason: Fall storms bring early snow to the 3,000-foot face and the park's backcountry permit season winds down in early October.

evidence: FA Aug 22, 1964 (Davis/Holland): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Booker_Mountain
NOCA backcountry fee season mid-May to early Oct (row's own access.fees).

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: August to September, when the crest and its west-side ledges are snow-free and dry for the long exposed traverse

June.reason: Snow still fills the Source Lake basin gully and clings to the north-side ledges of the crest, making the traverse slow and icy in spots.

July.reason: The approach gully melts out through the month; early July can leave snow patches on the crest and wet rock on the west-side bypasses.

August.reason: The ridge is dry and snow-free end to end, giving the most reliable conditions for the long, loose 4th-to-low-5th-class crest.

September.reason: Cooler, stable weather and a fully melted-out basin; shorter days matter on a traverse with few bail points, so start early.

October.reason: The first fall storms dust the crest with snow and verglas, which makes the loose rock and the short rappel off Bryant more serious.

evidence: Tooth-Chair traverse: 4th/low 5th, ~50 ft rappel off Bryant, 3-4 hrs on crest: https://www.mountainproject.com/route/119532399/tooth-chair-traverse

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: August to September, when the north-west crest is snow-free and settled dry weather firms up its poor rock

June.reason: The approach snow patch and the grassy gully over the ridge still hold snow, and the northwest-facing crest keeps wet, icy patches.

July.reason: The approach melts out and the ridge dries, though early July can leave snow in the gully to the route's start.

August.reason: The crest is at its driest, which matters most on runout pitches of loose rock where wet holds are the main danger.

September.reason: Settled early-fall weather and cool temperatures suit the six-pitch ridge; start early for the shorter days.

October.reason: Fall storms bring rain and early snow, and the northwest-facing ridge holds verglas that turns the runout pitches serious.

evidence: Chair Peak summer rock season May-Oct per SummitPost; snow patch on approach late June: https://www.summitpost.org/chair-peak/150834, https://gethighonaltitude.com/2023/06/23/chair-peak-voie-de-chaise/

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: August to September, after the Chair snow patch at the base melts back and the east-face slabs are dry

June.reason: The snow patch below the face still covers the start, often needing boots and an axe to chop steps to the first bolt.

July.reason: The snow patch shrinks through the month and the slabs dry; afternoon thunderstorms can build over the east face.

August.reason: The approach is mostly talus and scree and the bolted slab and crack pitches are reliably dry in the morning sun.

September.reason: Cooler, stable weather with the base fully melted out; the face goes into shade in the afternoon, so bring a layer.

October.reason: The route was established in the fall and climbs well on dry days, but the first storms coat ledges and the looser final pitches.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: July to August, when the entry couloir still holds firm snow early and the ridge crest above is dry

May.reason: The traverse to the base crosses snowy slabs with open glide cracks, and the entry couloir can still carry spring avalanche debris.

June.reason: Light crampons and an axe handle the snow in the entry couloir, but glide cracks on the approach slabs need care.

July.reason: The route was first climbed in late July: the approach slabs melt out, the couloir holds little snow and the crest is dry.

August.reason: The route goes to dry rock and crampons can usually stay home; the loose couloir sheds more rock once it is snow-free.

September.reason: Dry rock and cooler temperatures, but the melted-out entry couloir is at its loosest and the days shorten.

October.reason: Early fall snow in the couloir and verglas on the west-facing crest turn the short unprotected sections serious.

evidence: Light crampons/axe until mid-summer; snowy, glide-cracked approach early season: https://proguiding.com/blog/chair-peak-west-ridge-climb/

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: January to February, during a stable high-pressure spell when the hidden couloir's ice is formed and the snow above has settled

November.reason: The AI3 start is usually not yet formed and early-season snow sits unconsolidated on the rock of the northeast face.

December.reason: Ice can form in the entry couloir, but short days and the unplowed road to the Stuart Lake trailhead make for a very long approach.

January.reason: The first ascent came in late January during a long high-pressure spell, which freezes the ice pitches and settles the snow above.

February.reason: Mid-winter cold keeps the AI3 and M6 chimney in shape; wait for a stable spell after storms to limit avalanche hazard in the basin.

March.reason: Longer days help, but warm spells start to soften the snow slopes and load the Colchuck Lake basin with wet slide hazard.

April.reason: The ice start can still be climbable early in the month, but sun and warming rot the ice and raise avalanche and rockfall hazard.

May.reason: Spring melt strips the ice pitches and sheds rock down the face, and the overnight Enchantment permit season begins May 15.

evidence: FA Jan 2011 (Holsten/Hilden) during an uncommonly long high-pressure spell; AI3 start also climbed in April 2016: https://www.mountainproject.com/route/112066235/holsten-hilden

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Late July to mid-August, once the approach snow clears and before glacier bridges and the notch moat melt out

June.reason: The off-trail approach and ridge camps are still buried in snow, and the cracks on the east face drain meltwater.

July.reason: The approach clears through the month and glacier crossings are well bridged; early July can leave snow and ice on the lower pitches.

August.reason: The granite is dry and the Blue Glacier approach still goes, though bridges on the Chickamin crossing can melt out by late month.

September.reason: Dry rock and quieter weather, but the moat at the Middle-South notch widens and the glacier crossings become crevassed.

October.reason: Fall storms bring snow to the face and approach ridges, and the multi-day retreat through brush and glacier gets serious.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: July to August, once the saddle below the buttress melts out and before late-summer smoke and fire closures

May.reason: Snow still buries the meadows and cliff bands below the 6,200 ft saddle, and the bushwhack through avalanche debris is wet and slow.

June.reason: Snow is retreating from the south shoulder and patches still give water at the saddle bivy; the route has been climbed in late June.

July.reason: The southeast-facing rock is dry, the shoulder meadows are open, and long days help with the six-hour approach and slow, loose climbing.

August.reason: Reliably dry rock and snow-free cliff bands, but water above the meadows gets scarce and wildfire closures can shut the Hozomeen area.

September.reason: Stable weather often holds, but days shorten for a long bivy trip, water is scarce, and fire closures may still be in effect.

October.reason: Early snow and verglas on the upper buttress and the end of the backcountry permit peak season make this a late shoulder.

season_fix.best_season: Climbed June through September; the first ascent was made in late June. Mid-summer gives dry rock and a snow-free approach to the bivy saddle, while later in the season water is scarce and wildfire closures become likely.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: July, when the west basin and upper gullies are melting out but snowmelt water still runs above the basin

May.reason: Snow in the west basin eases the deadfall and gives water, but the rib/gully to the 6,800 ft saddle is still snow-loaded and the upper rock wet.

June.reason: Snowmelt still provides water at the 4,900-5,000 ft high camp and the gullies are clearing, though some steep snow may remain.

July.reason: The upper pitches are dry and mostly snow-free while late snow patches still supply water near the basin camp.

August.reason: Dry, snow-free rock, but water above the basin is often gone and late-summer wildfire can close the Hozomeen area.

September.reason: Settled weather is common but days are shorter, water must be carried from low, and fire closures may persist.

October.reason: Early-season snow and ice on the exposed upper mountain and cold, short days turn the loose rock into a serious undertaking.

season_fix.best_season: Climbed June through September. Earlier in the season, snowmelt supplies water on the approach and at the high camp; by late summer water above the basin is scarce and must be carried.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: January and February, when deep snow buries the brush and the north side holds its best snow for the skin up

November.reason: Early snow may not yet cover the brush and timber between FR 6700 and Lichtenwasser Lake, and the lake is not reliably frozen.

December.reason: The unplowed Smith Brook Road is usually packed for skinning and snow is filling in the forest, but early-winter slide cycles are common.

January.reason: Deep cover buries brush and talus, the lake is usually frozen to cross, and the north slopes hold good snow; watch for cornices on the ridge.

February.reason: Deepest snowpack and good north-side snow make the classic skin to the 5,640 ft saddle; check avalanche danger on both flanks.

March.reason: Longer days and still-deep snow, but warming raises wet-slide and cornice hazard, especially on the south side.

April.reason: The snowpack turns wet and heavy, the lake ice becomes unsafe, and brush starts to reappear low on the approach.

May.reason: Late spring brings rotten, unsupportive snow over buried ground and lingering wet-avalanche hazard on both flanks.

September.reason: A pleasant snow-free rock and heather scramble via the fishing trail, but a different outing from the ski line this route is known for.

evidence: Row best_season/beta: winter is the main season, north side better snow, avoid late spring; summer scramble Jul-Oct (first documented ascent Sept)

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: April to May, when long days meet a still-consolidated Cowlitz and Ingraham before summer opens their crevasses

January.reason: Glaciers are well filled in, but short days, frequent storms and gated winter access to Paradise make the traverse hard to fit in.

February.reason: The Cowlitz and Ingraham are covered and bridged; winter storm cycles and wind slab on the ramp to the face are the main concern.

March.reason: Deep, consolidated glacier cover with lengthening days; check for wind-loaded slopes on the ramp below the south/east face.

April.reason: Bridges are still solid across the traverse, days are long enough for the ski approach, and spring weather windows become more frequent.

May.reason: Long days allow a one-day ski ascent with an early start, but crevasses on the Cowlitz and Ingraham begin to open later in the month.

June.reason: The Cowlitz and Ingraham become broken and serac-threatened; most parties switch to the East Shoulder route from White River.

evidence: Typically done winter to early spring; glaciers too dangerous later; spring can be done in one long day on skis - https://www.mountainproject.com/route/122049367/cowlitzingraham-glaciers

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Late August through September, while the Yakama Nation opens the Bird Creek side to visitors; earlier holds more snow

June.reason: The Tract D area is closed to non-tribal visitors and the Bird Creek road is still snowbound.

July.reason: The headwall carries its best snow, but the reservation side usually stays closed to visitors until late summer.

August.reason: The Tract D area typically opens late in the month; the 45-degree headwall still holds snow though crevasses below Sunrise Camp open up.

September.reason: The most reliable month inside the visitor window; expect firm snow or ice on the headwall and open crevasses, and plan a long day-use push.

October.reason: The reservation area closes to visitors around October 1, and early storms ice the headwall.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: July to August, when the north face gullies and basin melt out and the rock dries

June.reason: Lingering snow covers some of the brushy lower spur, though the gully above the basin may still hold snow and the rib seeps.

July.reason: The basin and gully are mostly melted out and the North Rib pitches dry, with long days for a long route and brushy descent.

August.reason: The driest rock of the year on this shaded face; brush on the spur is fully exposed and the descent is slow.

September.reason: Rock usually stays dry but shorter days press on a long climb and descent; the first autumn rains return late in the month.

October.reason: Autumn rain keeps the north face wet and mossy, and early snow can dust the upper rib.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: August to September, when the shaded north face has finally dried out after the snowmelt

June.reason: Snow lingers at the base of the north face and the moss and cracks are still running with meltwater.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: June, while snow still covers the couloir and the brush below it, once the creek ford has dropped from its peak

August.reason: A dry, loose scree gully with no snow benefit; the summit is still reachable as a talus slog, and hot days make the long approach hard.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: July, when snow still bridges the moat at the buttress toe and the rock has dried out

May.reason: The Eightmile Road may still be gated by snow, the basin holds deep avalanche-prone snow, and the buttress is wet and snow-plastered.

June.reason: Continuous snow from the moraine gives an easy approach and a solid moat bridge, but late snow can linger on ledges and cracks may seep.

July.reason: The rock is dry, the glacier approach is still largely snow-covered and the moat is usually crossable on a snow block; long days suit a 17-hour push.

August.reason: Dry rock, but the moat at the toe opens wider and the glacier turns to bare ice, so the approach crossing and descent get harder.

September.reason: The moat can become a deep gap with no easy bridge, the glacier is bare ice, and shorter days force more of the descent by headlamp.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: April to May, when the spring snowpack has compacted over the cliff-band ramps and avalanche danger eases

December.reason: The turnout sits just west of the SR 20 winter gate so it is reachable, but deep unconsolidated snow and short days make the 5,500 ft gain slow.

January.reason: Deep winter snowpack on the open upper ridge and snow ramps through the cliff bands carries high avalanche hazard after storms.

February.reason: Storm loading keeps the upper ridge avalanche-prone; wait for a stable spell and firm snow before committing to the ramps.

March.reason: Longer days and a settling snowpack; the cliff bands are still turned on snow ramps, but watch for new-snow and warming avalanche cycles.

April.reason: Compact spring snow makes the steep timbered ridge and cliff-band ramps faster and generally lower-risk than deep winter snow.

May.reason: Firm morning snow on the upper ridge with long days; start early, as afternoon warming softens the ramps and triggers wet slides.

June.reason: The lower ridge melts out to steep brushy forest and the cliff-band ramps thin, losing the snow line this route depends on.

evidence: Turnout 12 mi E of Newhalem at ~1900 ft, just before the MP 134 winter closure gate; NW ridge is the winter/spring line: https://stephabegg.com/trip-reports/washington/ruby/
April 2017 NW Ridge route: https://cnmtstuartclimbproject.blogspot.com/2017/04/route-ruby-mountain-nw-ridge-route.html
April 2024 winter route: https://www.lucasmountainknowledge.com/post/ruby-mountain-april-2024
flags: Row hazard says the winter highway closure adds mileage; research puts the turnout just west of the winter gate, so it is normally drivable in winter. The hazard line may be overstated.
best_season wording 'while SR 20 is closed to vehicles beyond the gate' is fine; the window Dec-May matches it.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Late May to June, once the Eightmile Road opens and while the couloir still holds continuous firm snow

March.reason: The Eightmile Road is gated, adding miles on snow; the couloir holds snow but winter storm slabs and icy upper sections are common.

April.reason: A long ski or snowshoe in from the road gate; spring warming brings wet slides and sun-softened snow in the couloir by midday.

May.reason: The couloir is filled with consolidated snow or neve; the road opens as snow clears, and an early start avoids sluff and rockfall.

June.reason: The road is usually open and the couloir still holds continuous snow, but it may be hard or icy after a freeze; bring pickets and a second tool.

July.reason: The couloir melts out in patches, exposing loose rock and runnels; rockfall off the walls increases as it thaws.

August.reason: Largely a loose rock gully by now with high rockfall hazard; the snow line this route is named for is gone.

evidence: Route description: 1,200 ft couloir, 35-50 deg, neve or ice after freeze/thaw: https://www.summitpost.org/n-e-couloir/165520
Late March 2024 ski ascent, hard icy upper couloir: https://engineeredforadventure.com/sherpa-peak-ne-couloirs/
Row access: FR 7601 gated ~Nov-May

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: July to September, when the gully is dry and the chockstones and South Spur can be climbed on dry rock

May.reason: Rotting snow still fills the gully above cliffs; wet slides and loose rock released by melt make this the worst of both versions.

June.reason: The gully is mostly melted out, but lingering snow patches and wet, mossy chockstones can make the crux slick.

July.reason: Dry rock around the chockstones and on the South Spur; start early, as the south face gets hot and parties in the gully knock rock down.

August.reason: Dry and short from the parking lot; the fractured rock is at its most stable, but rockfall from parties above is the main hazard.

September.reason: Still dry most days with cooler temperatures; fall rain can make the chockstones and moss slick.

October.reason: Climbable between storms, but wet rock and early snow can return quickly and days are shorter.

December.reason: Once the gully fills and consolidates it becomes a snow and mixed climb to 50 degrees, with serious avalanche hazard below cliffs.

January.reason: The winter version: firm snow can bury the chockstones, but storm loading and nearby ski-area control work demand a stable forecast.

February.reason: Winter snow and mixed conditions; avalanche hazard in this south-facing gully rises sharply after new snow or warming.

evidence: MP summer/fall route, graded Easy 5th, II, 800 ft: https://www.mountainproject.com/route/111722458/south-gullysouth-spur
MP winter/spring version is a separate entry graded AI1-2 M2+ Mod. Snow: https://www.mountainproject.com/route/118581881/south-gullysouth-spur
Mountaineers trip reports: popular in winter, 50 deg snow: https://www.mountaineers.org/activities/trip-reports/intermediate-alpine-climb-guye-peak-south-gully-south-spur-1

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: August to September, after the Headlee Pass gully melts out and the vegetated ridge has dried

June.reason: The Mountain Loop Highway has usually reopened, but Headlee Pass is still a steep snow gully demanding self-arrest skill and the ridge is wet.

July.reason: Snow lingers in the Headlee Pass gully early in the month; the ridge dries out, though the vegetated rock stays damp after rain.

August.reason: Headlee Pass is usually snow-free and the heavily vegetated ridge is at its driest, which matters most on this low-quality rock.

September.reason: Dry, cooler days with the approach snow-free; the ridge is reliable between the first fall rains.

October.reason: Fall rain soaks the vegetation that covers the holds, early snow can return to Headlee Pass, and access roads can become snowbound.

evidence: Headlee Pass requires snow travel/self-arrest early; area main season Jul-Oct; MLH reopens ~Memorial Day: https://besthikesbc.ca/vesper-peak/
Sunrise Mine Trail 2.7 mi to Headlee Pass 4,720 ft: https://www.wta.org/go-hiking/hikes/sperry-peak
Row best_season: Summer and fall, needs dry rock
flags: Stored 'Summer-Fall' converted to Jul-Sep; October kept as a marginal shoulder.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: June, when consolidated snow fills the Great Basin and couloirs and links the rock sections between the two summits

April.reason: Deep, often unconsolidated snow on the ridge and in the Great Basin, with spring avalanche cycles on the steep snow descent.

May.reason: The snowpack is settling and the couloirs are filled, but cornices and wet afternoon snow on the steep descent into the Great Basin need care.

June.reason: Consolidated snow gives solid footing on the descent into the Great Basin and the final couloir, and the moats are small.

July.reason: Snow thins and moats open at the rock-snow transitions; early starts keep the snow pitches firm and reduce rockfall.

August.reason: Much of the snow linking the traverse is gone, leaving loose rock, open moats and a harder, less protected route.

evidence: Traverse is committing, north-to-south recommended, snow traverse demands respect: https://www.summitpost.org/the-brothers/517714
Traverse overview and topo: https://www.summitpost.org/the-brothers-traverse-and-the-south-summit/889751
Mountaineers route page (403 on fetch): https://www.mountaineers.org/activities/routes-places/the-brothers-brothers-traverse
flags: Could not fetch month-specific sources (403); breakdown built from the row's June recommendation and general Olympic snowpack pattern. Worth a look.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: July, while some snow still eases the Sawtooth Pass chute but the chimney pitch is dry

June.reason: Deep snow lingers around Flapjack Lakes and in the Sawtooth Pass chute, and the chimney can still be wet or icy.

July.reason: Lingering snow in Sawtooth Pass makes the chute easier and more stable, while the chimney pitch has dried out.

August.reason: The route is dry, but the pass chute and the rock above it get looser as the last snow melts off.

September.reason: Dry and quieter, but the Sawtooth Pass slope is at its most loose and the days are shorter for a long single-day push.

October.reason: Fall storms can bring early snow and wet rock to Sawtooth Ridge, and short days leave little margin on the long approach.

evidence: More snow = easier; chossy later in season: https://www.mountainproject.com/route/124501856/the-fin-northeast-face
NPS Flapjack Lakes trail: https://www.nps.gov/olym/planyourvisit/flapjack-lakes-trail.htm

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: July to early August, while snow bridges the glaciers and the moat below the face but the granite is dry

June.reason: The long off-trail approach is still under deep snow, which eases the brush but makes the glacier slog long and the high rock snowy.

July.reason: Snow still covers most crevasses and bridges the moat at the base of the face, while the granite has dried out.

August.reason: Dry rock, but crevasses open on the glaciers and the moat below the west face widens, making the start harder to reach.

September.reason: The moat below the face can become a deep gap with no easy crossing, the glaciers are icy, and shorter days stretch the approach.
